rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate the elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The intermediate temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Test a substantial temperature shift at the same gradient to separate the early critical cluster through selectivity changes. Higher temperature should also preserve or improve the current sub-10-minute last elution.

Make the gradient shallower at the best temperature to test whether the remaining critical pair gains resolution. The current 8.06-minute last peak leaves some room to spread peaks before the time penalty starts.

The remaining critical pair lost resolution with a shallower gradient, so test a steeper gradient instead. This also shortens elution, while checking whether the neighboring pair retains adequate resolution.

Shift the initial organic fraction upward while keeping the slope close to the best run, testing a new selectivity lever for the persistent critical pair. The first peak was retained well beyond the dead time, providing room for this window shift.

The maximum CRF is achieved; now test whether shortening the gradient preserves full resolution while reducing elution time. Keep the successful starting composition and temperature fixed to isolate the effect of gradient duration.

Reduce the gradient slope slightly to recover the small resolution deficits in injection 6, targeting full resolution with faster elution than injection 5. The final organic fraction remains comfortably above the last peak’s estimated elution composition.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction can shorten elution while preserving the selectivity gains seen at phi0 0.15. This explores a faster fully resolved method, with injection 7 retained as the current shortest maximum-score method.

Test a small temperature adjustment on the faster method whose two critical pairs narrowly missed full resolution. This isolates temperature-dependent selectivity while retaining ample margin below the 10-minute time-penalty threshold.

Test a slope between injections 6 and 7 to approach the fastest fully resolved boundary. The lower endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution composition, so all compounds should still elute during the gradient.

Explore the opposite temperature extreme for a different elution order and potentially better critical-pair selectivity; the small decrease to 55 C was unfavorable but does not rule out improvement after a crossover. The steep gradient and high endpoint should keep the last peak within 10 minutes.

Return to 60 C and test a shallower gradient at phi0 0.20 to recover the single deficient pair from injection 8. This checks whether the shifted window offers an alternative fully resolved method with greater separation of the other critical pair.

Slightly reduce the slope from injection 12 to bring its remaining R = 1.47 pair above 1.5. This targets another maximum-score method while retaining a comfortable margin below the 10-minute time penalty.

With maximum CRF already established, test whether a shallower gradient at the successful starting composition increases the critical-pair resolution margin. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, potentially providing a more robust maximum-score method.

Trim the endpoint and gradient duration while using a slope between two fully resolved runs. This should preserve full resolution with a shorter programmed gradient; the last compound may elute just into the final hold.

Raise the endpoint one step from injection 15 to shorten last-peak elution while retaining its resolution margin. This brackets the fastest fully resolved six-minute gradient against injection 10, whose critical pair remained just below 1.5.

Test whether modest cooling offsets early-peak compression at phi0 0.20 while preserving its improved separation of the next pair. This checks a temperature–starting-composition interaction not covered by the previous temperature tests.

Test the remaining starting-composition grid point between 0.05 and 0.15 to check for a better balance between the two critical pairs. Keep 60 C and a slope near the fastest fully resolved method to focus this comparison on early-cluster selectivity.

Preserve injection 7’s successful slope but end the gradient earlier, testing whether a shorter programmed gradient can retain maximum CRF. The late compounds will elute during the hold, so their retention times will determine whether this endpoint is sufficient.

Test the remaining endpoint step between injections 6 and 7 to locate the fastest fully resolved eight-minute gradient. The critical pair is near its resolution threshold, so retain injection 7 if this small slope increase loses full credit.

Back off one endpoint step from the fastest fully resolved method to increase its narrow critical-pair margin. This targets maximum CRF with only a modest increase in last-peak time relative to injection 7.

Use the fully resolving slope from injection 15 with a higher endpoint so the last peak remains inside the gradient. This should retain maximum CRF and a modest resolution margin without the hold-related broadening of that run.

Refine around the original maximum-score method by lowering its endpoint one step, aiming for a slightly larger critical-pair resolution margin. This should preserve full resolution and keep the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes.

Make injection 17’s gradient shallower to lift both nearly resolved critical pairs above 1.5, testing a fully resolved alternative at 55 C. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, while injection 7 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Lower the endpoint one step to recover the small remaining resolution deficit at 55 C, with last elution expected below 10 minutes. Maximum CRF is already secured, and injection 7 remains the fastest confirmed method with every pair at R ≥ 1.5.
